=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s assessment

**Do not accept this package as drafted.** It combines broad disclosure and deemed buyer knowledge with restrictions applying to *all Claims*. Together, those provisions could leave Wattlebridge bearing identified risks while having little effective recourse.

The Seller’s “[STANDARD]”, “FINAL” and “already agreed” labels are negotiating assertions—not evidence of Buyer approval or instructions limiting our review. Any actual principal-level agreement should be checked against the Buyer’s authorised deal record. The asserted “market” ranges do not establish that these terms suit this transaction.

This assessment is based on the supplied extracts, not the full SPA or underlying DD documents. Those documents need checking before settling drafting.

## 1. Completion protections and price integrity

### Bluefen: consent must be effective, not merely delivered
**Material risk:** Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6 million, or 30% of FY26 revenue**. The disclosure says no final consent or evidence of satisfaction of associated conditions has been provided. Written consent alone may not satisfy clauses 11.2–11.3.

**Push back:**
- Require a completion condition for valid, effective consent, with all associated conditions satisfied and no materially adverse variation, fee, termination right or other concession unless approved by the Buyer.
- Require the underlying evidence, not simply the Seller’s assertion that consent has been obtained.
- No unilateral Seller deeming of satisfaction. The Buyer should control waiver of this Buyer-protective condition and have appropriate long-stop termination rights.
- Reasonable endeavours is a process obligation, **not a substitute for the required outcome**.

### Riverlark: no unsecured promise to release after Completion
**Material risk:** Approximately **AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding**, with no final discharge of security. Acquiring the shares does not itself remove target debt or lender security.

**Push back:**
- Obtain an agreed lender payout statement, release documentation and an enforceable completion discharge mechanism covering relevant security and guarantees.
- Pay the lender directly through the completion funds flow where appropriate, against effective release arrangements. Any later administrative registration should be supported by binding lender obligations.
- Reflect the debt in the debt-free/cash-free price mechanics **once only**. Do not pay AUD 24 million to the Seller and leave the Company to fund the debt.
- Address any change-control default or lender consent separately; repayment arrangements do not automatically resolve every facility requirement.

### Completion bonuses: allocate the economic burden expressly
**Material risk:** The **AUD 420,000** conditional bonuses are omitted from the funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not prevent the Company—and economically the Buyer—from paying them after Completion.

**Push back:**
- Allocate these transaction-triggered bonuses to the Seller, whether paid directly where appropriate or captured as a clearly defined debt-like/transaction-expense deduction.
- Determine applicable superannuation, payroll tax, withholding and other on-costs, payment timing and continued-employment conditions.
- Include clear payment obligations, evidence and protection against residual Company liability.
- Avoid double counting against working capital, debt or another price adjustment.

First confirm whether the SPA uses completion accounts, a locked box or another mechanism; the treatment must work within that structure.

## 2. Known risks need targeted protection—not just disclosure

### Ironquay: protect ownership and use of the relevant IP
**Material risk:** Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open, but does not independently prove non-payment. Neither payment evidence nor a confirmatory assignment is available.

**Push back:**
- Reconcile all SOW3 fees and obtain reliable payment evidence.
- Require an effective confirmatory assignment and confirmation of relevant rights, including any necessary contributor chain of title and rights to embedded third-party materials.
- If material to the business, resolve ownership before Completion rather than relying solely on damages later.
- Broaden the specific indemnity beyond the identified payment to relevant pre-Completion ownership defects, third-party claims, remediation and interruption losses, subject to carefully drafted scope.
- Ensure disclosure, buyer knowledge and general warranty restrictions do not defeat that indemnity.

Paying AUD 180,000 alone may not cure every possible ownership defect; equally, the present record does not establish that ownership has definitively failed.

### Export/privacy incident: investigate before pricing or allocating it
**Material risk:** An unintended external recipient received a download link potentially covering approximately **1,240 records**. Access, scope and notification requirements remain unresolved. The Seller’s “not expected to be material” assessment is unsupported by the supplied evidence.

**Push back:**
- Require prompt investigation, preservation of logs, containment, identification of affected information and recipients, and a reasoned assessment of applicable notification obligations.
- Obtain appropriate investigation reporting, remediation commitments and updates through Completion.
- Consider a specific indemnity for losses arising from the pre-Completion incident, including reasonable investigation, notification, remediation and third-party claim costs, with regulatory amounts covered only to the extent legally permissible.
- Consider a retention or completion condition if the investigation reveals material exposure; maintain proportionate protections while uncertainty remains.

Do **not** describe this as a confirmed reportable breach or assign an invented loss figure. Uncertainty supports further investigation and risk allocation, not dismissal.

### Sandbar renewals: assess the aggregate commitment
**Material risk:** Three related renewals total **AUD 330,000**. The record does not establish whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary-course obligations.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together and obtain the contracts, renewal dates, cancellation rights, scope and approvals.
- Test compliance with pre-Completion conduct covenants and any related-transaction aggregation rules.
- Require Buyer approval for material new or renewed commitments before Completion.
- Decide accounting and price treatment from the facts. A genuine future operating expense is not automatically a Seller deduction; an undisclosed accrued liability or Seller-created extraordinary commitment may warrant different treatment.

## 3. Rewrite the liability architecture

| Provision | Buyer concern | Recommended position |
|---|---|---|
| **General warranty cap: AUD 4.8m / 20%** | It materially limits recovery; acceptability depends on diligence, residual exposure, security and the rest of the package. | Negotiate in context, not by reference to the Seller’s “market” label. Reserve separate treatment for fundamental warranties, tax and specific indemnities. |
| **AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 deductible basket** | Related small losses may escape; even eligible claims lose the first AUD 250,000. | Seek lower thresholds and a tipping basket. Aggregate related claims; specify whether de minimis claims count towards the basket. Exclude fundamental, tax and specific indemnity claims as appropriate. |
| **18-month general warranty period** | Some liabilities emerge only after a reporting or renewal cycle. | Seek a longer period matched to the business and diligence findings. Ensure timely notice preserves a claim even if loss is not yet quantified. Check any separate proceedings deadline. |
| **Capacity/title on general terms** | “Administrative simplicity” is no justification for limiting recovery where the Seller lacked authority or did not transfer good title. | Separate fundamental protections, ordinarily seeking a cap at least equal to the purchase price and materially longer survival, without ordinary warranty thresholds. |
| **Tax and IP within general regime** | Tax may emerge substantially later; core IP defects may threaten the acquired business. | Separate tax covenant/indemnity with appropriate statutory assessment-period coverage plus a buffer. Tailor IP protection to diligence, with specific treatment of Ironquay. |

### The “all Claims” extension is particularly dangerous

Clauses 9.3, 12.8, 20.5 and the proposed time-limit wording could extend warranty limitations to debt adjustments, payment obligations, covenants and specific indemnities. That would undermine protections negotiated elsewhere.

**Require:**
- Precise claim categories and an explicit schedule of which restrictions apply to each.
- Express protection for price adjustments, debt discharge and other payment obligations, fundamental claims, tax and specific indemnities.
- Appropriate fraud and deliberate-concealment carve-outs, with attribution carefully drafted.
- Preservation of rights and liabilities that cannot lawfully be excluded.
- No exclusive-remedy wording that unintentionally removes completion, termination or equitable remedies.

The effect of non-reliance and statutory exclusions requires NSW-law review. Do not assume a blanket clause either validly excludes every statutory remedy or is harmless because some exclusions may be ineffective.

## 4. Disclosure and buyer knowledge could hollow out the warranties

### Blanket data-room and public-record disclosure
General disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room is too broad. It may transfer risk without directing the Buyer to an intelligible exception.

**Push back:**
- Require fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of each matter, linked to the relevant warranty.
- Reject automatic disclosure of referenced but unavailable documents and unrestricted public-register material.
- Freeze and retain an indexed, accessible disclosure record.
- Prevent unilateral supplemental disclosures from curing warranty breaches or waiving Buyer rights.
- State expressly that disclosure does not qualify completion conditions, payment obligations or specific indemnities unless specifically agreed.

The letter’s factual qualifications are important, but disclosure is **not** consent, discharge, assignment, investigation completion or remediation.

### Constructive knowledge of the Buyer and all advisers
Clause 8.3 goes beyond actual knowledge to anything “discoverable”. That could make the warranties ineffective whenever the Seller argues the Buyer should have found the problem.

**Primary position:** delete the exclusion. If a compromise is necessary, confine it to actual conscious knowledge of named Buyer decision-makers, without deemed adviser knowledge or a duty to investigate. Ensure known-risk indemnities remain enforceable.

## 5. Verify title and avoid inventing consent requirements

- **Share title:** DD-012 is relevant evidence, not a substitute for verification. Check issued capital, ownership history, transfer restrictions, options and other equity rights, relevant encumbrances and completion transfer documents. Obtain unqualified title/capacity warranties and delivery of 100% of the shares free of encumbrances.
- **Office lease:** On this record, the obligation is notification—not landlord consent. Confirm timing and comply with the actual clause.
- **Mossvale:** An assignment restriction does not automatically apply to a share sale. Review the full agreement for a separate change-control or deemed-assignment provision before requiring consent.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Protect Completion:** effective Bluefen consent; Riverlark payout and release arrangements; verified clean share title.
2. **Protect the economics:** expressly allocate bonuses and on-costs, debt and transaction expenses without double counting.
3. **Resolve or allocate known risks:** Ironquay ownership, the export incident and the Sandbar commitments.
4. **Remove cross-cutting exclusions:** reject blanket “all Claims” restrictions, constructive knowledge and unrestricted disclosure.
5. **Then settle the general warranty package:** cap, thresholds and survival only after separate fundamental, tax and specific-risk protections are secured.

**Bottom line:** the central problem is not any single percentage. It is the combination of incomplete completion deliverables, unresolved liabilities and drafting that could exclude recovery for those same risks.
